analysis.one_liner: Cuts the interest rate cap on servicemembers' pre-service debts from 6% to 5% for three years.
analysis.headline: The bill to lower the interest cap for servicemembers from 6% to 5% never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already caps interest on debts a servicemember took on before entering the military at 6% during their service. This bill would have lowered that cap to 5% for the three years starting October 2006, reducing the interest active-duty troops owe on things like car loans, mortgages, and credit card balances they had before joining. It went to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers (and, on joint debts, their spouses) who carried debt into military service would pay one percentage point less interest on that debt for three years, saving them money on loans they took out before serving.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act so that, from October 1, 2006 through September 30, 2009, the maximum interest rate that may be charged on debts a servicemember incurred before entering military service is 5% instead of the current 6% [S2][S3].
The relief applies for the duration of the servicemember's military service and also covers debts incurred jointly with a spouse [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders — banks, credit card issuers, and finance companies holding loans made to people before they joined the military — would collect one percentage point less interest on those loans during the covered three-year period.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and consumer lenders holding those loans

drawbacks.text: The benefit is modest and temporary: it shaves one percentage point off the cap for only a three-year window, so a servicemember's total savings would be small, and after September 30, 2009 the cap returns to 6% [S2][S3].

Lenders could reasonably argue the change adds compliance cost and, for very small margins on some loans, could make them more cautious about extending credit to people about to enter military service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real but modest benefit: real money saved by servicemembers on pre-service debt, at a modest cost to lenders spread across many loans. It was a small, targeted improvement to an existing protection rather than a sweeping change, and its three-year sunset limited both the benefit and the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Ryun introduced the bill on December 15, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs [S1][S5].
On January 3, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it stayed; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders holding servicemembers' pre-service debts are better off, since the interest cap stayed at 6% and they kept collecting the extra interest. Servicemembers got no change at all.

against.name: Steve Buyer
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a hearing or a markup, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no clear partisan split can be measured from the record; the sponsor was a Republican [S4].

industries.industry: Consumer lenders (banks, credit card issuers, finance companies)
industries.note: They would have collected one percentage point less interest on loans to servicemembers during 2006-2009. Because the bill died, they kept the current 6% cap. Their interest ran against the troops who owed them money.
